pests.name: Cotton Bollworm / American Bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera)
symptoms: circular holes bored into squares, flowers, and bolls
premature shedding of squares and young bolls
larvae (caterpillars) visible inside damaged bolls when opened
damaged bolls open unevenly or rot

favorable_conditions.notes: Multiple overlapping generations in warm weather; population peaks during flowering and boll formation stages.

ipm_steps: Monitor with pheromone traps to track adult moth activity
Scout squares and bolls weekly for eggs and small larvae before they bore in
Encourage natural enemies such as Trichogramma wasps and predatory bugs
Use Bt cotton varieties where locally approved, as a resistance-management component, not a sole strategy
Practice crop rotation and destroy crop residue after harvest to reduce carryover
Apply targeted insecticide only when economic threshold is reached, and rotate modes of action to limit resistance
sources: ICAR Central Institute for Cotton Research advisories

pests.name: Pink Bollworm (Pectinophora gossypiella)
symptoms: rosette-shaped flowers caused by larvae feeding inside flower buds
small pin-holes in bolls with pink-colored larvae inside when opened
premature boll opening with lint stained pink or damaged
reduced fiber quality and seed damage

favorable_conditions.notes: Survives between seasons in old bolls and ginning waste, so infestation risk rises where crop residue is not destroyed.

ipm_steps: Destroy crop residue and unopened bolls after final harvest to break the pest's carryover cycle
Use pheromone traps for early detection of moth emergence
Avoid late-season irrigation or fertilization that extends boll formation into high-risk periods
Follow regional refuge crop guidelines if using Bt cotton, to slow resistance development
Time any insecticide application to early larval stages based on scouting, since larvae are protected once inside bolls
sources: ICAR Central Institute for Cotton Research advisories

diseases.name: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus (CLCuV)
symptoms: upward or downward curling of leaves
thickened, vein-like enations (outgrowths) on the underside of leaves
stunted plant growth and reduced boll formation
transmitted by whitefly, so whitefly presence is a strong contextual clue

favorable_conditions.notes: Risk closely tracks whitefly vector populations, which favor hot, dry conditions.

ipm_steps: Control whitefly populations as the primary transmission vector
Use resistant or tolerant cotton varieties where available
Remove and destroy severely infected plants early in the season
Avoid staggered planting dates near infected fields, which extends vector activity windows
Maintain field sanitation and avoid alternate weed hosts near field borders
sources: ICAR Central Institute for Cotton Research advisories

diseases.name: Bacterial Blight / Angular Leaf Spot (Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum)
symptoms: small water-soaked angular spots on leaves, bounded by veins
spots turn dark brown to black as they mature
black lesions along leaf veins and on stems (vein blight)
boll rot with dark sunken lesions in severe cases

favorable_conditions.notes: Favored by warm, humid, rainy weather and spread by wind-driven rain and contaminated seed.

ipm_steps: Use certified, disease-free or acid-delinted treated seed
Avoid working in fields when foliage is wet, since this spreads bacteria
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops for at least one season
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
Avoid excess nitrogen, which increases susceptibility
Apply copper-based bactericides preventively in high-risk wet weather if locally recommended
sources: ICAR Central Institute for Cotton Research advisories
